questions.learningObjective: Recognize that one character has variant forms
questions.stem: Item 0001: A dispatcher's log shows two glyphs for one character; what is the best reading?

options.text: They are variant forms of the same character with different stroke arrangements.
They are two completely unrelated characters that happen to look alike.
One is a typo that should be deleted from the log.
options.misconception: labels a variant as a typo

options.text: They are the same character printed in different fonts only.

questions.explanation: Two glyphs for one character are variant forms with different stroke arrangements. They are not unrelated characters, typos, or mere font differences.
questions.hint: Think variant forms, not unrelated glyphs.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The four-corner lookup method
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the four-corner method
questions.stem: Item 0002: Explain the purpose of the four-corner lookup method in a dispatcher's log.

answer.exemplar: The four-corner method assigns a number to each corner of a character so that unknown characters can be located in a dictionary even when their pronunciation is unknown.

questions.explanation: The method uses corner shapes to locate characters without knowing pronunciation. It is not a pronunciation or stroke-count tool.
questions.hint: It locates characters by corner shapes.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why one character carries several numbers
questions.learningObjective: Count corner numbers for a character

stimulus.body: A dispatcher's log lists a character whose four corners are numbered 1, 2, 3, and 4. The clerk must total the corner numbers.

questions.stem: Item 0003: What is the total of the four corner numbers?

options.text: The total is 24, from 1 times 2 times 3 times 4.
The total is 10, from 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4.
The total is 4, using only the last corner number.
The total is 1, using the smallest corner number.

questions.explanation: Adding 1, 2, 3, and 4 gives 10. Multiplication or using one corner are incorrect operations for this total.

A variant is always a typo; a different character is always intentional.
A variant shares the same character identity but differs in stroke arrangement; a different character has a distinct identity.

questions.explanation: A variant shares character identity but differs in stroke arrangement, unlike a distinct character. Typo, equivalence, and font-size explanations are wrong.

questions.stem: Item 0043: Should the clerk treat them as variants?

options.text: No, because any stroke difference creates a new character.
options.misconception: treats stroke differences as new characters

options.text: Yes, because shared meaning and pronunciation with differing strokes indicate variants.
No, because variants must be identical in every stroke.

questions.explanation: Shared meaning and pronunciation with differing strokes indicate variants. Stroke differences do not automatically create new characters, and variants need not be identical or same-font.
